key_findings: Sustainable power is roughly ⅓ of your best few-second power; trained cyclists hold ~80% of VO2max-test power for 30 minutes.
Even in steady state, glycolysis supplies 10–12% of ATP (up to ~20%) — and the acid it makes suppresses ADP, the signal that drives the mitochondria.
Mitochondria in sustained exercise run well below capacity: peak steady-state ADP is 0.06–0.11 mmol/L vs ~0.3 needed for full drive — oxygen isn't the limiter.
Full mitochondrial drive is reachable (quads at VO2max: ADP 0.25, pH 6.5) but sustainable for under 5 minutes.
Raising the ceiling means making less acid per watt and clearing it faster — the snake muscle that sustains >80% of capacity for hours has half-diameter fibres (33 vs 67 µm) and ~35% more blood flow.

header.title_plain: Why you can't hold your top aerobic pace: acid from glycolysis blunts the signal that drives the mitochondria

citation.title: Limits to sustainable muscle performance: interaction between glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation
citation.authors: Conley KE, Kemper WF, Crowther GJ

header.evidence_type: Review/hypothesis built on the authors' 31P-MRS studies of human muscle and rattlesnake tail-shaker muscle, plus cited literature. NIH and NSF funded.

confidence.why: A coherent mechanistic argument, partly validated in an animal model.

practical_relevance.why: Mechanism paper with one actionable framing (sustainable pace is set by acid build-up, which endurance adaptations reduce); hand entry said low–medium, low chosen.

review.claim: The power you can sustain for more than a few minutes is set inside the muscle, by whether ATP supply can match demand. Even in fully aerobic steady-state exercise, glycolysis supplies a sizeable share of ATP and so produces acid (H+). That acid lowers the concentration of ADP, which is the signal that tells mitochondria how hard to work. So mitochondria in sustained exercise run well below their capacity — not because oxygen is short, but because the activating signal is suppressed. Three phases follow: fatiguing high power (seconds), a transitional zone (seconds to minutes, PCr and pH drifting down), and the sustainable zone.

evidence_cited.finding: Sustainable power is a fraction of max
evidence_cited.numbers: ~⅓ of maximal power sustainable for prolonged periods; cyclists hold ~80% of their VO2max-test power for 30 min

evidence_cited.finding: Glycolysis contributes to steady-state ATP in humans
evidence_cited.numbers: 10–12% of ATP from glycolysis producing lactate; up to ~20% including the glycolytic step on the way to oxidation; vs 8% expected if all pyruvate were oxidised
Glycolysis >⅓ (~40%) of sustained ATP; MRS estimate matched direct lactate measurement

evidence_cited.finding: Mitochondria are not fully switched on in steady state
evidence_cited.numbers: Highest steady-state ADP in muscle 0.06–0.11 mmol/L; ~0.3 mmol/L needed to elicit full oxidative capacity. Steady-state PCr falls only to ~half resting
PCr down to 3 mmol/L, pH 6.5, ADP 0.25 mmol/L — near maximal mitochondrial drive, sustainable <5 min

evidence_cited.finding: Keeping pH high is the other route
evidence_cited.numbers: pH 7.2 (vs 6.5 in human quads at VO2max), PCr 10 mmol/L, ADP 0.15 → >80% of oxidative capacity, sustained. Achieved by fibres half the diameter (33 vs 67 µm) and blood flow 468 vs 350 ml/100 g/min in human athletes

evidence_cited.finding: Oxygen isn't the limiter at steady state
evidence_cited.numbers: O2 delivery may limit near VO2max in athletes, but not at the lower rates of steady-state work; glycolysis is independent of oxygenation in stimulated human muscle

evidence_cited.finding: PCr recovery slows at low pH

review.untested_or_contested: Whether pH acts on the ADP signal or directly on mitochondria. The argument is a "contention" supported by MRS; direct whole-body confirmation isn't available.

layer2.what_it_means: This is the physiology behind the lactate/anaerobic threshold, told from inside the cell. Your sustainable pace isn't capped by the lungs or the heart at that intensity; it's capped by acid accumulation turning down the mitochondria's throttle. Two things raise the ceiling: fewer H+ produced per unit of work, and faster H+ removal — the snake does it with tiny fibres and enormous blood flow. In human terms that's the rationale for the adaptations endurance training produces (more capillaries, more mitochondria, better buffering and lactate clearance), and it explains why the threshold, not VO2max, tracks what you can actually hold.
layer2.what_it_doesnt_mean: It's a mechanism paper with no training intervention and one validated animal model; the human numbers are from small MRS studies of single muscles. It doesn't tell you how to raise the threshold, only what sets it. Don't read "glycolysis supplies 10–20% of steady-state ATP" as "steady-state exercise is 20% anaerobic" in the sense coaches use — the lactate produced is largely re-oxidised. And the ⅓-of-max and 80%-for-30-min figures are illustrative, not prescriptive.

translation: Sustainable power ≈ ⅓ of your best few-second power; ~80% of VO2max-test power holds for ~30 min in cyclists.
What limits it: acid build-up dampening the signal to the mitochondria, not oxygen supply.
What raises it: producing less acid per watt and clearing it faster — the adaptations endurance training targets.

glossary_candidates.definition: What's left when ATP is spent; its rise is the signal that tells mitochondria to make more ATP.
The mitochondrial process that makes ATP using oxygen.
Exercise at an intensity where PCr, pH and oxygen uptake stop drifting — sustainable for long periods.
Acidity inside the muscle fibre; falls (acid rises) with hard work and interferes with energy signalling.
The muscle's capacity to absorb acid; improves with training.
How many small blood vessels surround each fibre; more means faster delivery of oxygen and removal of acid.
